question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Kansas?

## Direct Answer
You find a fractional CRO in Kansas through three main channels: specialized fractional-executive networks (Chief Outsiders, Fractionals United, Bolster), Kansas-focused RevOps and sales-leadership communities in Kansas City, Wichita, and Topeka, and warm referrals from your investors, PEG partners, or fellow founders. Vet on B2B GTM track record, industry fit, and time commitment before signing — location matters far less than pattern-match to your revenue problem.

Hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer in Kansas is less about finding someone with a Kansas ZIP code and more about finding a senior revenue operator who fits your stage, sector, and growth ceiling. Most fractional CROs work remotely or hybrid, so a Wichita manufacturer or an Overland Park SaaS startup can realistically hire the same caliber of leader as a coastal company — often at a fraction of the fully loaded cost of a full-time hire. The trick is knowing which channels surface real operators versus resume-padders, and how to run a disciplined vetting process once you have a shortlist.

## What is a fractional CRO and when does a Kansas company actually need one?
A fractional CRO is a senior revenue executive who owns your go-to-market strategy — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, pricing, and forecasting — but works part-time, typically one to three days a week, on a fixed monthly retainer instead of a full-time salary plus equity. They are pattern-matchers: people who have already built and scaled revenue engines multiple times and can compress a year of trial-and-error into a quarter of focused execution. For a Kansas company, the appeal is straightforward. You get VP- and C-level revenue leadership without a $300K-plus base, without the recruiting lag, and without betting the whole company on one full-time hire who may not fit.

The clearest signals that you need one: revenue has plateaued and your founder-led sales motion no longer scales, you are raising a round and investors want a credible GTM leader in the seat, your sales team is missing quota without a diagnosable reason, or you are entering a new segment and lack the playbook to attack it. Kansas has a deep bench of B2B companies — agtech and precision-agriculture firms, aerospace and advanced manufacturing suppliers around Wichita, logistics and distribution operators along the I-70 and I-35 corridors, and a growing Kansas City SaaS and fintech cluster — that hit exactly these inflection points. A fractional CRO fits because these companies are big enough to need real revenue leadership but often not yet large enough to justify a full-time CRO's cost. If you want to sanity-check whether the timing is right, our breakdown at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-readiness walks through the readiness gate.

## Where do I actually find fractional CRO candidates in Kansas?
There are four channels that reliably surface qualified operators, and they work best in combination rather than in isolation. The first is dedicated fractional-executive platforms and networks. Firms like Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Continuum, Go Fractional, and Fractionals United maintain vetted rosters of part-time revenue leaders and will match you to two or three candidates based on your stage and industry. These platforms handle the initial screening, which saves you the top-of-funnel grind, but you still own the final vetting. The second channel is your own network — investors, your private-equity or search-fund sponsor if you have one, your board, your accountant, and other founders. Warm referrals consistently produce the highest-quality candidates because the referrer is staking their reputation on the intro.

The third channel is Kansas-specific professional communities. The Kansas City chapters of Pavilion (formerly Revenue Collective), the RevGenius and Wichita Regional Chamber networks, KU and Kansas State alumni founder groups, and local RevOps meetups are all places where fractional operators surface. LinkedIn Sales Navigator, filtered to "Fractional CRO" or "Fractional Chief Revenue Officer" within a Kansas or Kansas City radius, is a legitimate fourth channel — many of the best fractional leaders market themselves directly and skip the platforms entirely. The diagram below maps the typical sourcing flow from need to signed engagement.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Revenue plateau or GTM gap] --> B[Define the mandate and success metrics]
    B --> C[Fractional networks]
    B --> D[Warm referrals from investors and founders]
    B --> E[Kansas RevOps and Pavilion communities]
    B --> F[LinkedIn direct outreach]
    C --> G[Shortlist of three to five candidates]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Structured vetting and reference checks]
    H --> I[Paid trial or pilot sprint]
    I --> J[Signed retainer engagement]
```

A practical note on geography: do not over-index on finding someone physically in Kansas. The strongest fractional CROs for a Kansas company are the ones who have scaled revenue in your specific motion — whether that is field sales into manufacturers, product-led growth for SaaS, or channel and distribution. A remote operator with exact pattern-match beats a local generalist almost every time. If in-person quarterly business reviews or on-site sales-team coaching matter to you, make that an explicit requirement and screen for it, rather than letting proximity silently narrow your pool. Our sourcing playbook at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-executive-sourcing goes deeper on channel-by-channel yield.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost in Kansas, and how is it structured?
Fractional CRO compensation is almost always a monthly retainer tied to a defined day-commitment, not an hourly rate and not a full salary. The retainer scales with seniority, the number of days per week, and the scope of the mandate. A lighter advisory engagement — one day a week, strategy and cadence oversight — sits at the lower end, while a hands-on operator running your sales team two to three days a week commands considerably more. Because these figures move with market conditions, seniority, and scope, get live quotes from three candidates rather than anchoring to a single number; the spread between an advisory seat and an embedded operator is wide enough that a blind assumption will mislead your budget.

Structurally, the smart move is to tie a portion of the engagement to outcomes. Many fractional CRO agreements blend a base retainer with a performance component — a bonus on hitting pipeline, bookings, or net-revenue-retention targets, or in some cases a small equity or advisory-share grant for early-stage companies that want to conserve cash. Kansas companies, particularly bootstrapped or PEG-backed ones, often prefer the cash-plus-performance structure because it aligns incentives without diluting ownership. Whatever the shape, insist on a defined term (a 90-day initial engagement is common), clear success metrics agreed up front, and a clean off-ramp. The comparison below frames the trade-off against a full-time hire.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Revenue leadership need] --> B{Full time or fractional}
    B -->|Full time CRO| C[High base plus equity]
    C --> D[Long recruiting cycle]
    C --> E[Full risk on one hire]
    B -->|Fractional CRO| F[Monthly retainer]
    F --> G[Days per week flexible]
    F --> H[Fast start and easy off ramp]
    G --> I[Lower total cost]
    H --> I
```

The cost logic is why fractional works so well at the lower-middle-market scale common in Kansas: you are buying the top 10 percent of revenue-leadership judgment for a fraction of the days, and you can dial the commitment up or down as the company grows. When the company outgrows the fractional model, a good fractional CRO will often help you recruit and onboard the full-time replacement — which is exactly how the engagement should end.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I do not get burned?
Vetting is where most companies either succeed or waste six months. Start with track record, not title. Ask each candidate to walk you through two or three specific revenue turnarounds they personally led — what the starting numbers were, what they changed, what the numbers became, and what did not work. Vague answers about "driving alignment" and "building culture" are a red flag; real operators talk in pipeline coverage ratios, win rates, sales-cycle compression, and net revenue retention. Pattern-match their history to your actual problem: someone who scaled enterprise field sales is the wrong hire if your bottleneck is a self-serve PLG funnel.

Second, check references hard, and check them off-list — talk to a former CEO the candidate worked under and, ideally, a rep who reported to them, not just the two names they hand you. Ask the reference the uncomfortable question directly: would you hire this person again, and what would you warn me about? Third, confirm capacity. A fractional CRO juggling six clients cannot give you real attention; ask how many active engagements they carry and how many days a week you are actually buying. Fourth, run a paid trial. A two- to four-week diagnostic sprint — where the candidate audits your funnel, sits in on real deals, and delivers a written 90-day plan — tells you more than any interview. You see how they think, how they write, and whether your team responds to them before you commit to a longer term. Our vetting scorecard at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vetting gives you a structured rubric to run this process consistently.

Finally, get the mandate and the metrics in writing before day one. The single biggest cause of failed fractional engagements is a fuzzy scope — the company expected a hands-on team leader, the CRO thought they were an advisor, and neither realized the mismatch until a quarter was gone. Define exactly what "success" means in 90 days, what decisions the fractional CRO owns versus recommends, and what access to the team and data they get. Clarity up front is the cheapest insurance you will buy in the entire engagement.

## Fractional CRO versus fractional VP of Sales versus RevOps consultant — which do I need?
These three roles overlap enough to cause expensive confusion, so it is worth separating them. A fractional CRO owns the entire revenue architecture: sales, the marketing-to-sales handoff, RevOps and systems, pricing, forecasting, and the go-to-market strategy across the whole funnel. You hire a CRO when the problem is strategic and cross-functional — when marketing, sales, and success are not aligned and no single leader owns the number end to end. A fractional VP of Sales, by contrast, is narrower and more tactical: they own the sales team, the pipeline, quota attainment, and rep coaching. You hire a VP of Sales when your strategy is sound but execution inside the sales org is broken.

A RevOps consultant is different again — they fix the machinery underneath revenue: your CRM hygiene, your reporting and dashboards, your lead routing, your comp-plan mechanics, and your tech stack. You hire a RevOps consultant when your data is a mess and you cannot trust your own forecast, regardless of whether strategy or execution is the deeper issue. Many Kansas companies actually need a sequence rather than a single role: a fractional CRO to set strategy and diagnose, who then either directs a RevOps cleanup or hands off day-to-day execution to a VP of Sales once the architecture is in place. If you are unsure which seat you are trying to fill, our role-comparison guide at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-vs-vp-sales-vs-revops maps symptoms to the right hire so you do not overpay for a strategist when you needed a mechanic, or vice versa.

## Related questions
### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most start with a 90-day initial term to prove value, then convert to a rolling monthly or quarterly retainer. Typical total engagements run six to eighteen months — long enough to install a durable revenue engine, short enough to avoid becoming a permanent crutch.

### Can a fractional CRO work fully remotely for a Kansas company?
Yes. The large majority of fractional CROs work remotely or hybrid, using regular video cadences, CRM access, and periodic on-site visits. If you need in-person team coaching or quarterly on-site reviews, make that an explicit requirement when you screen candidates.

### Do fractional CROs work with early-stage startups or only established companies?
Both, but the mandate differs. Early-stage startups usually want help finding repeatable go-to-market and building the first playbook; established companies want to break a plateau or enter a new segment. Confirm the candidate's history matches your stage.

### Should I hire through a network or find a fractional CRO independently?
Networks like Bolster or Chief Outsiders save screening time and de-risk the first pass, but they add a markup. Independent hires via referral or LinkedIn cost less and can fit better, but you own all the vetting. Many companies run both channels in parallel.

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and an interim CRO?
A fractional CRO is permanent-but-part-time — a few days a week indefinitely. An interim CRO is full-time-but-temporary, usually filling a gap while you recruit a permanent hire. Choose interim when you need a full-time seat covered now; choose fractional when part-time senior leadership is genuinely enough.

## FAQ
**Are there fractional CROs based specifically in Kansas City, Wichita, or Topeka?**
Yes — the Kansas City metro in particular has a growing bench of fractional revenue leaders, and you will find operators around Wichita's manufacturing and aerospace cluster too. Use Pavilion KC, local RevOps meetups, and LinkedIn geo-filtered searches to surface them. That said, do not restrict yourself to local candidates if a remote operator is a better pattern-match to your revenue problem.

**How quickly can a fractional CRO start delivering value?**
A strong fractional CRO delivers a diagnostic and a prioritized 90-day plan within the first two to three weeks, because they are pattern-matching against problems they have already solved. Meaningful pipeline or process improvement typically shows within the first quarter. If a candidate cannot articulate what they would assess in week one, that is a warning sign.

**What should be in a fractional CRO contract?**
At minimum: the day-per-week commitment, the monthly retainer and any performance component, a defined initial term (90 days is standard), explicit success metrics, scope of authority (what they own versus advise on), data and team access, confidentiality and IP terms, and a clean termination clause with notice period. Get the mandate in writing before day one.

**Will a fractional CRO manage my existing sales team directly?**
It depends on the mandate you set. Some fractional CROs run the sales team hands-on, including one-on-ones and deal coaching; others operate at the strategy layer and direct your existing sales manager. Decide which you need before you hire, because a mismatch here is the most common cause of failed engagements.

**Can a fractional CRO help me hire my eventual full-time CRO?**
Yes, and the best ones expect to. A well-run fractional engagement often ends with the fractional CRO writing the role spec, defining the scorecard, interviewing candidates, and onboarding the full-time replacement they helped you find. Build that transition into the scope from the start.

**How is a fractional CRO different from a management consultant?**
A consultant analyzes and recommends, then leaves you to execute. A fractional CRO is an embedded operator who owns outcomes — they sit in your revenue meetings, make decisions, and are accountable to the number, not just to a deck. If you want a diagnosis you will implement yourself, hire a consultant; if you want someone accountable for results, hire a fractional CRO.

**Is a fractional CRO worth it for a company under $5M in revenue?**
Often yes, precisely because such companies need senior revenue judgment but cannot justify a full-time CRO's cost. The key is buying the right number of days — usually one to two per week at that scale — and tying the engagement to concrete milestones so the spend is disciplined and measurable.
